info.text: An operational amplifier is a high-gain differential amplifier whose useful circuits come from how that gain is used: tamed by negative feedback into a precise linear stage, or left open-loop so the output slams to a rail as a decision.

citations.title: Operational Amplifiers and Linear Integrated Circuits: Theory and Application
citations.author: James M. Fiore

clusters.name: Ideal model
clusters.fact: For analysis, an ideal op-amp senses only the voltage between its differential-input pins, multiplies that difference by a huge open-loop gain, and draws negligible input current because its input impedance is treated as infinite.

differential input.text: The op-amp responds to the voltage difference between its non-inverting (+) and inverting (−) terminals, not to either terminal's voltage alone.

termInfo.infinite input impedance: The idealization that no current enters either input pin, so the surrounding network—not the amplifier—sets all input-node currents.

open-loop gain.text: The raw voltage gain from the differential input to the output with no feedback path connected; at low frequency it is typically 10^5 or more.

clusters.name: Linear feedback circuits
clusters.fact: With the output feeding back to the inverting input, resistor ratios—not the op-amp's raw gain—set a precise closed-loop gain: an inverting amplifier flips polarity, a non-inverting amplifier preserves it, and a virtual short between the inputs makes that arithmetic valid.

termInfo.closed-loop gain: The controlled voltage gain of the amplifier with the feedback network connected, ideally set by external resistors rather than by open-loop gain.

inverting amplifier.text: A closed-loop op-amp circuit that produces an output inverted relative to the input, with gain set by the ratio of feedback to input resistance.

non-inverting amplifier.text: A closed-loop op-amp circuit that amplifies without inverting polarity; its ideal gain is 1 plus the feedback-to-ground resistor ratio.

virtual short.text: The analysis condition that the two input pins sit at almost the same potential, even though no real wire shorts them and no current flows between them.

clusters.name: Comparison and switching
clusters.fact: Used without a linearizing feedback network, the same high-gain device becomes a comparator: a tiny input difference drives the output to a rail, and a Schmitt trigger adds hysteresis so noise cannot chatter the trip point.

Schmitt trigger.text: A comparator with different rising and falling thresholds, produced by positive feedback, so the output snaps cleanly instead of oscillating around one level.

comparator.text: A circuit that outputs one of two saturation levels according to which of two input voltages is larger, interfacing a continuous analog difference to a digital-like decision.

termInfo.hysteresis: A gap between the upper and lower thresholds, so the reference that must be crossed depends on the present output state.
termInfo.trip point: The input voltage at which the comparator output changes state; with hysteresis there are distinct upper and lower trip points.

clusters.name: Real-device limits
clusters.fact: A real op-amp cannot keep the idealizations: slew rate caps how fast the output can move, gain-bandwidth product spends high-frequency open-loop gain, input offset voltage appears as a false DC difference, and the output voltage swing stops short of the supplies.

gain-bandwidth product.text: The nearly constant product of open-loop gain and frequency for a compensated op-amp, equal to the unity-gain frequency; closed-loop bandwidth shrinks as closed-loop gain rises.

input offset voltage.text: The differential DC voltage that must be applied between the inputs to force the output to zero; it is amplified by the circuit's DC gain and shows up as output offset.

termInfo.output voltage swing: How close the output can actually get to the supply rails before clipping; it is less than the full supply span on ordinary op-amps.

slew rate.text: The maximum rate of change of output voltage, usually given in volts per microsecond, which distorts large or fast waveforms even when small-signal bandwidth looks adequate.

bridges.fact: Negative feedback returns a portion of the output to the inverting input so the huge open-loop gain drives the differential input toward zero, producing the virtual short that lets resistor ratios set closed-loop gain.

info.text: A loop that subtracts a sample of the output from the input, reducing gain in exchange for a controlled, stable response.

citations.title: 3.2: What Negative Feedback Is and Why We Use It
citations.author: James M. Fiore

bridges.fact: Saturation is the same rail-limited output in two roles: it is the failure of a linear amplifier whose feedback can no longer keep the output proportional, and it is the intended high or low state of a comparator.

info.text: The condition in which the output has reached its maximum or minimum voltage, set by the supplies and the output stage, and can no longer follow the input.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts name the feedback and the closed-loop circuits that keep the output proportional to the input?
lenses.explanation: Negative feedback holds the device in the linear region so resistor networks can set a closed-loop gain. An inverting amplifier and a non-inverting amplifier are the two standard ways to do that. Open-loop gain is what gets tamed; it does not by itself keep the output proportional. A comparator leaves that region on purpose.

reasons.closed-loop gain: It is the proportional factor those circuits are designed to set.
reasons.inverting amplifier: It is a closed-loop circuit whose output is a scaled, inverted copy of the input.
reasons.negative feedback: It is the loop that trades raw gain for a controlled, proportional response.
reasons.non-inverting amplifier: It is a closed-loop circuit whose output is a scaled copy that keeps the input's polarity.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts are the real-device limits that keep an op-amp from matching its ideal model?
lenses.explanation: The idealizations treat gain, speed, and input balance as unlimited and the output as free to go wherever the math says. A datasheet answers with slew rate, gain-bandwidth product, input offset voltage, and a finite output voltage swing. Saturation is the resulting rail-stuck state, not one of those named limits.

reasons.gain-bandwidth product: It spends open-loop gain against frequency, so a higher closed-loop gain has less remaining bandwidth.
reasons.input offset voltage: It is a false DC difference at the inputs, so the output is not zero when the signal is.
reasons.output voltage swing: It stops short of the supplies, so the output cannot reach the voltages an ideal model allows.
reasons.slew rate: It caps how fast the output can move, so large or fast signals distort even when the small-signal model looks fine.

info.text: Op-amp circuits sit between network laws that set resistor ratios and feedback used as a control idea rather than as an analog building block.

entries.reason: The closed-loop gains here are resistor ratios; circuit theory is where series connections and voltage division get their own board.
Negative feedback appears there as a process-control loop with a setpoint and actuator, not as the analog trick that creates a virtual short.
